Title: Rick Scott on Hurricane Irma: 'Our state has never seen anything like it'
Chunks: 0,1,2
Sept. 9, 2017 Updated Sept. 10, 2017, 1:25 a.m. ET
Gov. Rick Scott flew to southwest and central Florida Saturday, grimly urging residents to get out of evacuation zones as killer Hurricane Irma’s outer winds reached the Florida Keys.
“There will be 18 to 15 inches of rain across the state and up to 25 inches in the Keys,” Scott warned during a briefing at the State Emergency Operations Center Saturday evening. “Tornadoes are possible in South Florida this evening and Central Florida tomorrow.”
He said storm surge as high as 15 feet is expected. Scott said forecasts call for 5-to-8-foot storm surges in the Tampa area and three to six feet in the Big Bend.
Irma could hit Big Bend as a major hurricane
Local shelters, comfort stations: How to prepare now for Hurricane Irma
Leon County officials issued a voluntary evacuation call at mid-afternoon “due to the increasing likelihood of hurricane-force winds for an extended period of time.” The mammoth hurricane is expected to reach the Big Bend late Sunday night or early Monday.
“This is clearly a life-threatening situation,” Scott said.
The cavernous EOC near Southwood was abuzz all day, with scores of employees coordinating the evacuation of millions from South Florida. Overhead video screens constantly updated Irma’s track across Cuba’s northern coastline, projecting its northward turn near Fort Myers.
The storm’s likely path — casting the entire peninsula under a hurricane watch or warning — appeared to edge westward along the Gulf of Mexico as it slowly moved north.
“I want to be clear,” Scott said in Orlando, “we are under a state of emergency. This is a catastrophic storm. It’s bigger than our state.”
Irma’s winds were estimated at more than 155 miles an hour. An estimated 6.4 million Floridians live in the southern evacuation zones, but state officials could not estimate how many left and how many took refuge in more than 200 shelters.
Scott did a series of television interviews on national news shows in the morning at the EOC, before flying south. He returned in the afternoon for briefings by heads of state and federal agencies, power companies, public health officials and others who have been through storms before — but never like Irma.

Scott’s message to residents in coastal areas was brutally blunt: Get out. Major highways were bumper-to-bumper as residents fled inland and northward.
Although Scott suspended load limits and had Highway Patrol officers escorting fuel trucks into the state Friday and early Saturday, gasoline shortages were everywhere. Hundreds of drivers ran out and left cars on roadsides.
The state set up an emergency phone line at (800) 342-3557, and Scott said rescue workers would come to the aid of people who were unable to evacuate on their own “for whatever reason.” But he warned that once high winds and storm surge began, law enforcement would not be able to venture out until the storm passed.
Scott also called for 1,000 volunteer nurses to serve in storm shelters. He said 25,000 south Floridians had already lost electricity when he held his 9 a.m. briefing in Sarasota.
“The storm is here,” Scott said as tropical storm winds lashed the Keys. “This is a deadly storm and our state has never seen anything like it. Millions of Floridians will see major hurricane impacts with deadly storm surge and life-threatening winds.”
**Earlier story:**
With a sense of urgency in his voice, Gov. Rick Scott bluntly told millions of Floridians in a mammoth evacuation zone to leave or take shelter immediately today, as Hurricane Irma’s high winds began battering the Keys.
“The storm is here,” Scott said at a briefing in the Sarasota Emergency Operations Center. “This is a deadly storm and our state has never seen anything like it. Millions of Floridians will see major hurricane impacts with deadly storm surge and life-threatening winds.”
The governor said 25,000 south Floridians had already lost electricity when he held his 9 a.m. briefing.
Irma weakened to a Category 4 hurricane after striking northern Cuba overnight, but was forecast to strengthen back to Category 5 — with winds of more than 150 miles an hour — in the warm Straits of Florida waters as it curves north to the Keys.
The projected path inched westward Friday night, putting Tallahassee squarely in the right hemisphere of Irma’s destructive swirl. Storm surge warnings of six to 12 feet extended as far up the Gulf coast as Cedar key.

“You need to leave now,” Scott said, enunciating each word slowly for emphasis. “Do not wait, evacuate — not tonight, not in an hour, you need to leave now.”
The governor said the state has an emergency service number — 800 342-3557 — for anyone wanting to evacuate, but having problems finding or reaching a shelter. He said “we will do everything we can” to help people before the hurricane hits — but emphasized that once Irma strikes, law enforcement officers will not be able to venture out in it.
“I want to be clear,” Scott said, “we are under a state of emergency. This is a catastrophic storm. It’s bigger than our state.”

He returned in the afternoon for briefings by heads of state and federal agencies, power companies, public health officials and others who have been through storms before — but never like Irma.

Scott’s message to residents in coastal areas was brutally blunt: Get out. Major highways were bumper-to-bumper as residents fled inland and northward.
Although Scott suspended load limits and had Highway Patrol officers escorting fuel trucks into the state Friday and early Saturday, gasoline shortages were everywhere. Hundreds of drivers ran out and left cars on roadsides.
The state set up an emergency phone line at (800) 342-3557, and Scott said rescue workers would come to the aid of people who were unable to evacuate on their own “for whatever reason.” But he warned that once high winds and storm surge began, law enforcement would not be able to venture out until the storm passed.
Scott also called for 1,000 volunteer nurses to serve in storm shelters. He said 25,000 south Floridians had already lost electricity when he held his 9 a.m. briefing in Sarasota.

Title: Gov. Scott urges patience in wake of Irma
Chunks: 0,1
Updated Sept. 11, 2017, 5:34 p.m. ET
Gov. Rick Scott flew to ravaged areas of South Florida Monday, urging Floridians to be patient about returning to their homes and warning of the continued danger of flooding and hot power lines in the trail of Hurricane Irma.
“It’s horrible, what we saw,” Scott said at a news conference in Opa-locka, after flying over the Florida Keys and Gulf coast counties to survey the devastation. “I know for our entire state, but especially the Keys, it’s going to be a long road.”
Businesses, restaurants open in Tallahassee after Hurricane Irma
Hurricane Irma damage in Florida: City by city
Scott made the rounds of morning network news shows, appearing by video or telephone, and filled his day with phone calls to state and federal disaster-recovery officials. Wearing his familiar Navy ball cap, he joined Vice Admiral Karl Schultz aboard a Coast Guard C-130 cargo plane in Mobile, Alabama, —while Irma's remnants were still deluging North Florida with heavy rains and tropical storm-force winds — and flew to Monroe County.
After his stop at a Coast Guard air base in Opa-locka, Scott scheduled a visit to a public shelter at Imokalee High School.
Scott said 65 percent of the state lost electricity during Irma’s overnight onslaught Sunday and early Monday. He said utility companies are sending some 23,000 workers into the state to expedite reconnections, but it’s going to take time because Florida has never had a hurricane that enveloped the entire peninsula and much of the Big Bend and Panhandle with storm surge, punishing winds and flooding.
He said Monroe County had a 10-foot initial storm surge at landfall, while Miami-Dade County had four feet and the Tampa area experienced surges of two to four feet. The Big Bend experienced storm surge of three to six feet, he said.
More than a foot of rain fell in the Orlando and Jacksonville areas. Flooding in the port city was aggravated by storm surge of three to five feet, on top of more than 12 inches of rain fall, while Hurricane Juan out in the Atlantic pushed water shoreward – causing “record and historical flooding along the St. Johns River.”

“Don’t think just because this has passed you can run home,” said Scott. “We’ve got downed power lines all across the state, we’ve got roads that are impassable all over the state, we’ve got debris all over the state.”
Scott said Port Everglades and the Port of Tampa reopened as soon as possible after Irma and gasoline shipments resumed with Highway Patrol escorts.
The governor praised the work of federal, state and local employees, along with military and public-health volunteers.
“Everybody is working their tails off,” Scott said. “Unfortunately, everybody’s going to have to be patient because it’s going to be a lot of work to get this done.”
Schultz said the Department of Homeland Security “has been preparing for Irma to arrive, first in the Caribbean and then here in Florida, for a good part of more than a week. The Coast Guard has been reconstituting our forces here in Florida.”

9/9/2017
**TALLAHASSEE, Fla.**– Today, Governor Rick Scott received a full update on Hurricane Irma from the State Emergency Operations Center. The Governor has traveled the state this week to meet with local officials, ensure communities have all the resources they may need, and to encourage families and visitors to be fully prepared. The Governor will continue to be in constant communication with state and local emergency management officials, city and county leaders, and utility officials who are also working to ensure the state is prepared to respond to Hurricane Irma.
**EMERGENCY SUPPORT FUNCTIONS BY STATE EMERGENCY RESPONSE TEAM**
**WATCHES AND WARNING –**
*   Storm Surge Warning

    *   Santee River southward around the Florida peninsula to  the Suwanee River  
    *   Florida Keys  
    *   Tampa Bay

*   Storm Surge Watch

    *   North of the Suwanee River to Ochlockonee River

*   Hurricane Warning

    *   Fernandina Beach southward around the Florida peninsula  to Indian Pass  
    *   Florida Keys  
    *   Lake Okeechobee  
    *   Florida Bay  
    *   Cuban provinces of Camaguey, Ciego de Avila, Sancti  Spiritus, Villa Clara, Matanzas, and Havana  
    *   Andros Island, Bimini and Grand Bahama

*   Hurricane Watch

    *   North of Fernandina Beach to Edisto Beach

*   Tropical Storm Warning

    *   West of Indian Pass to the Okaloosa/Walton County Line  
    *   North of Fernandina Beach to South Santee River
**EVACUATIONS**
_Though the below evacuation orders are current and in effect, everyone should check with their local emergency management office or website for the most up to date information regarding evacuation as they are constantly being updated._

Updated Sept. 11, 2017, 5:34 p.m. ET
Gov. Rick Scott flew to ravaged areas of South Florida Monday, urging Floridians to be patient about returning to their homes and warning of the continued danger of flooding and hot power lines in the trail of Hurricane Irma.
“It’s horrible, what we saw,” Scott said at a news conference in Opa-locka, after flying over the Florida Keys and Gulf coast counties to survey the devastation. “I know for our entire state, but especially the Keys, it’s going to be a long road.”
Businesses, restaurants open in Tallahassee after Hurricane Irma
Hurricane Irma damage in Florida: City by city
Scott made the rounds of morning network news shows, appearing by video or telephone, and filled his day with phone calls to state and federal disaster-recovery officials. Wearing his familiar Navy ball cap, he joined Vice Admiral Karl Schultz aboard a Coast Guard C-130 cargo plane in Mobile, Alabama, —while Irma's remnants were still deluging North Florida with heavy rains and tropical storm-force winds — and flew to Monroe County.
After his stop at a Coast Guard air base in Opa-locka, Scott scheduled a visit to a public shelter at Imokalee High School.
Scott said 65 percent of the state lost electricity during Irma’s overnight onslaught Sunday and early Monday. He said utility companies are sending some 23,000 workers into the state to expedite reconnections, but it’s going to take time because Florida has never had a hurricane that enveloped the entire peninsula and much of the Big Bend and Panhandle with storm surge, punishing winds and flooding.
He said Monroe County had a 10-foot initial storm surge at landfall, while Miami-Dade County had four feet and the Tampa area experienced surges of two to four feet. The Big Bend experienced storm surge of three to six feet, he said.
More than a foot of rain fell in the Orlando and Jacksonville areas. Flooding in the port city was aggravated by storm surge of three to five feet, on top of more than 12 inches of rain fall, while Hurricane Juan out in the Atlantic pushed water shoreward – causing “record and historical flooding along the St. Johns River.”

“Don’t think just because this has passed you can run home,” said Scott. “We’ve got downed power lines all across the state, we’ve got roads that are impassable all over the state, we’ve got debris all over the state.”
Scott said Port Everglades and the Port of Tampa reopened as soon as possible after Irma and gasoline shipments resumed with Highway Patrol escorts.
The governor praised the work of federal, state and local employees, along with military and public-health volunteers.
“Everybody is working their tails off,” Scott said. “Unfortunately, everybody’s going to have to be patient because it’s going to be a lot of work to get this done.”
Schultz said the Department of Homeland Security “has been preparing for Irma to arrive, first in the Caribbean and then here in Florida, for a good part of more than a week. The Coast Guard has been reconstituting our forces here in Florida.”
